label: Variability is induced by changed conditions acting on the reproductive system
claim: Deviations of structure arise in some way from the conditions of life to which parents and their ancestors have been exposed over several generations, acting chiefly by disturbing the reproductive system; hence variability is greater under domestication or cultivation than in nature.
quote: But the much greater variability, as well as the greater frequency of monstrosities, under domestication or cultivation, than under nature, leads me to believe that deviations of structure are in some way due to the nature of the conditions of life, to which the parents and their more remote ancestors have been exposed during several generations.
scope: plants and animals, domesticated and wild
measurable_quantities: phenotypic variance of domesticated vs wild conspecifics
frequency of developmental abnormalities under captive vs wild conditions
variance in offspring traits after environmental change of parents
candidate_data: Comparative morphometric datasets of domestic breeds and their wild ancestors (e.g. dog and pigeon morphometrics on Dryad); plant common-garden and transplant experiments.

label: Direct effects of climate and food on organisms are small
claim: The direct effect of differences in climate, food and similar conditions on an organism's structure is very small in animals and perhaps somewhat larger in plants, and cannot account for the complex co-adaptations between organisms.
quote: How much direct effect difference of climate, food, etc., produces on any being is extremely doubtful. My impression is, that the effect is extremely small in the case of animals, but perhaps rather more in that of plants.
scope: plants and animals in nature
measurable_quantities: magnitude of phenotypic plasticity in response to temperature or diet
plasticity effect sizes in animals vs plants
candidate_data: Meta-analytic datasets of phenotypic plasticity from reciprocal-transplant and common-garden experiments, many archived on Dryad; TRY plant trait database for within-species trait variation across environments.

section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
label: Flightlessness of birds on predator-free oceanic islands is caused by disuse
claim: The nearly wingless condition of several birds living on oceanic islands that lack beasts of prey has been caused by disuse of the wings.
quote: I believe that the nearly wingless condition of several birds, which now inhabit or have lately inhabited several oceanic islands, tenanted by no beast of prey, has been caused by disuse.
scope: birds of oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: incidence of flightlessness on islands with vs without mammalian predators
relative wing size in island vs mainland relatives
candidate_data: AVONET avian morphology database and bird phylogenies (BirdTree) for island vs mainland wing-length comparisons; subfossil records of extinct flightless island birds.

section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
label: Wingless Madeira beetles result mainly from selection against being blown to sea
claim: The high proportion of flightless beetles on windswept islands such as Madeira is mainly due to natural selection favouring individuals that fly least and so avoid being blown out to sea, probably combined with disuse.
quote: these several considerations have made me believe that the wingless condition of so many Madeira beetles is mainly due to the action of natural selection, but combined probably with disuse.
scope: insects of oceanic islands, especially ground-living beetles
measurable_quantities: proportion of flightless insect species per island
wind exposure of islands
wing reduction in ground-feeding vs flower-feeding island insects
candidate_data: Island insect checklists with flight-capability traits (e.g. published datasets on flightlessness in island insects, including sub-Antarctic and Macaronesian faunas) combined with climate data on wind speed.

section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
label: Blindness in cave animals results from disuse
claim: Because useless eyes are unlikely to be harmful in total darkness, the loss of eyes in most cave-dwelling animals is due to disuse alone rather than to natural selection.
quote: As it is difficult to imagine that eyes, though useless, could be in any way injurious to animals living in darkness, I attribute their loss wholly to disuse.
scope: cave-dwelling animals
measurable_quantities: rate of eye regression in cave vs surface lineages
energetic cost of eye tissue in darkness
signatures of selection on eye-related traits in cave populations
candidate_data: Cave fish (Astyanax mexicanus) comparative and experimental datasets; GenBank/SRA sequence data for cave and surface populations of cave-dwelling taxa.

section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
label: Cave animals are related to surface fauna of their own continent
claim: Blind cave animals of America should be most closely allied to other inhabitants of America, and those of Europe to inhabitants of Europe, rather than the cave faunas of the two continents being specially similar to each other.
quote: Notwithstanding such modifications, we might expect still to see in the cave-animals of America, affinities to the other inhabitants of that continent, and in those of Europe, to the inhabitants of the European continent.
scope: cave faunas of North America and Europe
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic sister-group relationships of cave taxa
phylogenetic distance between cave taxa and local surface relatives vs cave taxa on other continents
candidate_data: Molecular phylogenies of cave beetles, amphipods and fish from GenBank and Open Tree of Life.

label: Species ranges are limited by competition as much as by climate
claim: Species in nature are limited in their geographic ranges by competition with other organisms at least as much as, or more than, by adaptation to particular climates.
quote: We have reason to believe that species in a state of nature are limited in their ranges by the competition of other organic beings quite as much as, or more than, by adaptation to particular climates.
scope: plants and animals in nature
measurable_quantities: climatic niche breadth of native range vs naturalised range
performance of species transplanted beyond range limits
range-limit position relative to climatic tolerance
candidate_data: GBIF occurrence records combined with WorldClim climate layers for native vs introduced ranges; GloNAF naturalised alien flora database; published transplant experiments beyond range limits.

label: Homologous parts tend to vary together
claim: Parts of the body that are homologous and alike early in embryonic development, such as left and right sides or fore and hind limbs, tend to vary in a correlated way.
quote: The several parts of the body which are homologous, and which, at an early embryonic period, are alike, seem liable to vary in an allied manner
scope: animals and plants with serially or bilaterally homologous parts
measurable_quantities: phenotypic correlation between homologous vs non-homologous traits
covariation of fore- and hindlimb dimensions
candidate_data: Morphometric datasets of limb and skeletal measurements (e.g. mammal and bird skeletal datasets on Dryad and MorphoSource) analysed for morphological integration.

label: Taxonomically important characters may be useless products of correlated growth
claim: Structural differences that systematists treat as highly important, such as differences between outer and inner seeds of Umbelliferae, may arise entirely from unknown laws of correlated growth without being of any use to the species.
quote: Hence we see that modifications of structure, viewed by systematists as of high value, may be wholly due to unknown laws of correlated growth, and without being, as far as we can see, of the slightest service to the species.
scope: plants and animals; characters used in classification
measurable_quantities: fitness effects of diagnostic characters
correlation of diagnostic characters with other developing structures
candidate_data: Plant trait databases (TRY) and phylogenies to test whether taxonomically diagnostic fruit or seed traits are correlated with adaptive traits; few direct datasets known.

label: Natural selection reduces superfluous parts without compensatory enlargement
claim: Natural selection will in the long run reduce any part of the organisation once it becomes superfluous, saving nutriment, without necessarily causing another part to enlarge; and it can enlarge an organ without requiring reduction of an adjoining part.
quote: Thus, as I believe, natural selection will always succeed in the long run in reducing and saving every part of the organisation, as soon as it is rendered superfluous, without by any means causing some other part to be largely developed in a corresponding degree.
scope: all organisms, e.g. parasitic cirripedes losing the carapace
measurable_quantities: rate of loss of unused structures in parasitic or sheltered lineages
correlation between reduction of one organ and enlargement of others
candidate_data: Phylogenetic comparative datasets on trait loss in parasites and cave or island lineages; experimental-evolution datasets (e.g. LTEE, Dryad) on loss of unused functions.

section: Multiple, rudimentary, and lowly organised structures variable.
label: Parts repeated many times in an individual are variable in number
claim: When a part or organ is repeated many times in one individual, such as snake vertebrae or stamens of polyandrous flowers, its number is variable, whereas parts present in small numbers are constant in number.
quote: when any part or organ is repeated many times in the structure of the same individual (as the vertebræ in snakes, and the stamens in polyandrous flowers) the number is variable; whereas the number of the same part or organ, when it occurs in lesser numbers, is constant.
scope: plants and animals with serially repeated parts
measurable_quantities: within-species coefficient of variation in part counts
mean part count per individual
candidate_data: Vertebral count datasets for snakes and fishes and floral organ counts from herbarium and flora databases (e.g. published Dryad datasets on vertebral number variation).

section: Parts developed in an unusual manner are highly variable: specific characters more variable than generic: secondary sexual characters variable.
label: Parts unusually developed relative to congeners are highly variable
claim: A part developed to an extraordinary degree or in an extraordinary manner in one species, compared with the same part in closely allied species, tends to be highly variable within that species; the rule does not apply when the unusual part is shared by a whole group.
quote: _A part developed in any species in an extraordinary degree or manner, in comparison with the same part in allied species, tends to be highly variable_.
scope: animals, especially birds, cirripedes and secondary sexual characters; Darwin could not confirm it for plants
measurable_quantities: within-species coefficient of variation of a trait
deviation of species trait mean from congeneric mean
candidate_data: Museum morphometric datasets for congeneric species (e.g. AVONET for birds) allowing comparison of trait variance against trait exaggeration relative to congeners.

section: Parts developed in an unusual manner are highly variable: specific characters more variable than generic: secondary sexual characters variable.
label: Specific characters are more variable than generic characters
claim: Characters that distinguish species within a genus are more variable within species than characters shared by all species of the genus, because the former have varied since the species branched from a common progenitor.
quote: It is notorious that specific characters are more variable than generic.
scope: species within genera of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: intraspecific variance of species-diagnostic vs genus-diagnostic characters
candidate_data: Taxonomic character matrices (e.g. MorphoBank) combined with intraspecific morphometric data from museum collections.

section: Parts developed in an unusual manner are highly variable: specific characters more variable than generic: secondary sexual characters variable.
label: Congeners differ more in secondary sexual characters than in other parts
claim: Secondary sexual characters are highly variable, and species of the same group differ from one another more in their secondary sexual characters than in other parts of their organisation.
quote: species of the same group differ from each other more widely in their secondary sexual characters, than in other parts of their organisation
scope: sexually dimorphic animals, e.g. gallinaceous birds
measurable_quantities: interspecific divergence in male ornament traits vs non-sexual traits
male vs female interspecific plumage divergence
candidate_data: Comparative plumage colour and ornament datasets for birds (e.g. published spectrophotometric plumage datasets on Dryad) with AVONET morphology and BirdTree phylogenies.

section: Species of the same genus vary in an analogous manner.
label: Related species with shared constitution produce analogous variations
claim: Species that inherit nearly the same constitution from a common parent and are exposed to similar influences tend to produce analogous variations, so that a variety of one species may resemble another species of the same genus.
quote: Species inheriting nearly the same constitution from a common parent and exposed to similar influences will naturally tend to present analogous variations
scope: species within a genus, domestic races and wild species
measurable_quantities: frequency of parallel variants across related species or breeds
phylogenetic signal in the occurrence of particular variants
candidate_data: Comparative data on parallel phenotypes in domestic breeds (pigeon, dog, chicken breed trait surveys) and phylogenetic studies of parallel evolution in wild taxa.

label: Long-lost characters reappear through a tendency transmitted each generation
claim: When a character lost in a breed reappears after many generations, the cause is a tendency to produce that character transmitted in every generation which at last prevails under favourable conditions, not a sudden resemblance to a distant ancestor.
quote: When a character which has been lost in a breed, reappears after a great number of generations, the most probable hypothesis is, not that the offspring suddenly takes after an ancestor some hundred generations distant, but that in each successive generation there has been a tendency to reproduce the character in question, which at last, under unknown favourable conditions, gains an ascendancy.
scope: domestic breeds and wild species
measurable_quantities: frequency of ancestral phenotypes (atavisms) among offspring of crosses between breeds
persistence of atavistic tendencies across generations
candidate_data: Pigeon and chicken breed crossing studies; experimental crosses archived on Dryad; none known as a single comprehensive dataset.

label: Horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra descend from a striped common ancestor
claim: The domestic horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra are descended from a common ancestor that was striped like a zebra, which explains the occasional appearance of stripes in horses, asses and their hybrids.
quote: For myself, I venture confidently to look back thousands on thousands of generations, and I see an animal striped like a zebra, but perhaps otherwise very differently constructed, the common parent of our domestic horse, whether or not it be descended from one or more wild stocks, of the ass, the hemionus, quagga, and zebra.
scope: genus Equus
measurable_quantities: monophyly of Equus
ancestral state reconstruction of striping
frequency of leg and shoulder stripes in horse breeds, asses and hybrids
candidate_data: Equid phylogenies from ancient and modern DNA in GenBank/SRA and Open Tree of Life; Paleobiology Database equid fossils; coat-pattern surveys of horse breeds.

section: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.
label: Formation of a new form exterminates its parent and transitional varieties
claim: Because each new form tends in a fully stocked country to supplant and exterminate its less improved parent and other competing forms, the parent and all transitional varieties are generally exterminated by the process that forms the new species.
quote: Hence, if we look at each species as descended from some other unknown form, both the parent and all the transitional varieties will generally have been exterminated by the very process of formation and perfection of the new form.
scope: all species in fully stocked regions
measurable_quantities: survival of ancestral or intermediate lineages after speciation
frequency of extant paraphyletic ancestral species
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database lineage durations and ancestor-descendant fossil series; molecular phylogenies from Open Tree of Life for budding vs replacement speciation patterns.

section: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.
label: Zones of overlap between representative species are narrow
claim: Where closely allied or representative species replace each other over a continuous area, the neutral territory between them is generally narrow compared with the territory occupied by each, and species become somewhat abruptly rarer towards their range limits.
quote: Hence the neutral territory between two representative species is generally narrow in comparison with the territory proper to each.
scope: representative species on continents, mountains and sea depths
measurable_quantities: width of contact or hybrid zones relative to range size
abundance gradient toward range edges
candidate_data: GBIF occurrence data and range maps (e.g. IUCN/BirdLife range polygons) for parapatric sister species; published hybrid-zone width compilations.

section: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.
label: Intermediate varieties are numerically rarer than the forms they connect
claim: Where varieties intermediate between two other forms occur in nature, they are generally much rarer numerically than the forms they connect, because they inhabit narrower intermediate zones.
quote: generally when varieties intermediate between two other forms occur, they are much rarer numerically than the forms which they connect.
scope: varieties of plants and animals in nature
measurable_quantities: abundance of intermediate phenotypes or hybrids vs parental forms
area occupied by intermediate forms vs parental forms
candidate_data: Hybrid-zone and cline studies with genotype or phenotype frequency transects (many archived on Dryad); GBIF abundance and occurrence data for subspecies.

section: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.
label: Common forms improve faster and supplant rare intermediate forms
claim: Forms existing in larger numbers have a better chance in any given period of presenting favourable variations for natural selection, so they are improved faster and supplant the less numerous intermediate varieties between them.
quote: For forms existing in larger numbers will always have a better chance, within any given period, of presenting further favourable variations for natural selection to seize on, than will the rarer forms which exist in lesser numbers.
scope: varieties and incipient species
measurable_quantities: rate of adaptation as a function of population size
persistence of small intermediate populations
candidate_data: Experimental-evolution datasets comparing adaptation rates across population sizes (e.g. microbial experiments on Dryad, LTEE-derived studies).

label: Bat flight arose from an apparatus for gliding
claim: Bats were derived from gliding animals, and the wing membrane extending to the tail and hind legs in some bats is a trace of an apparatus originally built for gliding rather than flight.
quote: In bats which have the wing-membrane extended from the top of the shoulder to the tail, including the hind-legs, we perhaps see traces of an apparatus originally constructed for gliding through the air rather than for flight.
scope: bats and gliding mammals
measurable_quantities: ancestral state reconstruction of patagium configuration
morphology of early fossil bats
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database records of Eocene bats; mammal phylogenies from TimeTree and Open Tree of Life; MorphoSource fossil scans.

section: Species with habits widely different from those of their allies.
label: Habits can change without corresponding change of structure
claim: Species sometimes have habits that do not match their structure, such as upland geese with webbed feet that rarely enter water or ground-living woodpeckers, showing that habits can change before structure changes.
quote: In such cases, and many others could be given, habits have changed without a corresponding change of structure.
scope: birds and other animals
measurable_quantities: mismatch between morphology and ecology across species
phylogenetic order of behavioural vs morphological shifts
candidate_data: AVONET morphology and EltonTraits foraging and habitat data combined with BirdTree phylogenies to detect ecomorphological mismatches.

label: Complex eyes can be built by selection through graded useful steps
claim: Natural selection could have converted a simple optic nerve coated with pigment and covered by transparent membrane into a highly perfect eye through a series of graded steps, each useful to its possessor, as shown by the graduated diversity of eyes in living crustaceans.
quote: I can see no very great difficulty (not more than in the case of many other structures) in believing that natural selection has converted the simple apparatus of an optic nerve merely coated with pigment and invested by transparent membrane, into an optical instrument as perfect as is possessed by any member of the great Articulate class.
scope: eyes of Articulata (arthropods and allies), extended to vertebrates
measurable_quantities: range of eye complexity among living related taxa
phylogenetic ordering of eye structures
candidate_data: Comparative eye morphology across invertebrates in published phylogenetic studies; Open Tree of Life phylogenies for ancestral-state reconstruction.

label: Theory fails if a complex organ could not arise by slight steps
claim: If any complex organ were shown to exist that could not possibly have been formed by numerous, successive, slight modifications, the theory of natural selection would break down; no such case is known.
quote: If it could be demonstrated that any complex organ existed, which could not possibly have been formed by numerous, successive, slight modifications, my theory would absolutely break down.
scope: complex organs of all organisms
measurable_quantities: existence of documented intermediate stages for complex organs
candidate_data: Fossil series in the Paleobiology Database and comparative phylogenetic studies of organ evolution; none known as a single dataset.

label: Lung-bearing vertebrates descend from an ancestor with a swimbladder
claim: All vertebrates with true lungs have descended from an ancient ancestor that had a swimbladder used for flotation, which natural selection converted into a lung.
quote: I can, indeed, hardly doubt that all vertebrate animals having true lungs have descended by ordinary generation from an ancient prototype, of which we know nothing, furnished with a floating apparatus or swimbladder.
scope: vertebrates
measurable_quantities: ancestral state of air-filled organs in bony fishes
phylogenetic position of lunged vs swimbladder-bearing lineages
candidate_data: Vertebrate phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) with comparative anatomy of lungs and swimbladders; Paleobiology Database early osteichthyan fossils.

label: Selection can independently produce similar organs in distantly related beings
claim: Natural selection, acting on analogous variations, has sometimes modified parts in nearly the same way in two distantly related organisms, as with electric organs in unrelated fishes, so that similar organs need not be inherited from a common ancestor.
quote: so natural selection, working for the good of each being and taking advantage of analogous variations, has sometimes modified in very nearly the same manner two parts in two organic beings, which owe but little of their structure in common to inheritance from the same ancestor.
scope: electric fishes, luminous insects, orchids and Asclepias, and other cases of similar organs in remote groups
measurable_quantities: number of independent origins of a trait on a phylogeny
structural differences between convergent organs
candidate_data: Fish phylogenies (Fish Tree of Life, Open Tree of Life) for mapping origins of electric organs; insect phylogenies for bioluminescence.

label: Few organs lack any known transitional grade
claim: Despite the small proportion of living and known forms relative to extinct and unknown ones, it is rare to find an organ toward which no transitional grade is known to lead.
quote: I have been astonished how rarely an organ can be named, towards which no transitional grade is known to lead.
scope: organs of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: proportion of organs with known intermediate states in living or fossil relatives
candidate_data: Comparative anatomical character matrices (MorphoBank) and fossil series in the Paleobiology Database.

label: Nature makes no leaps when past as well as present forms are included
claim: The rule that nature makes no leaps is not strictly true of living organisms alone, but if all past organisms are included it must be strictly true.
quote: This canon, if we look only to the present inhabitants of the world, is not strictly correct, but if we include all those of past times, it must by my theory be strictly true.
scope: all organisms, living and extinct
measurable_quantities: morphological gaps between living taxa vs gaps when fossil taxa are included
rates of morphological change in fossil lineages
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database and morphological character matrices combining fossil and extant taxa (MorphoBank) to measure morphospace gaps.

label: Traits from laws of growth are later co-opted by descendants
claim: Many modifications arose wholly from laws of growth and were at first of no advantage to a species, but were later taken advantage of by its further modified descendants, as skull sutures that arose in egg-laying animals were later used in mammalian birth.
quote: we may confidently believe that many modifications, wholly due to the laws of growth, and at first in no way advantageous to a species, have been subsequently taken advantage of by the still further modified descendants of this species.
scope: plants and animals
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic timing of trait origin vs origin of its current function
candidate_data: Phylogenetic comparative datasets with ancestral-state reconstructions of trait and function (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree combined with trait matrices).

label: Most of an organism's structure is due to inheritance, not current use
claim: The chief part of each organism's structure is simply inherited, so that many structures, such as the shared bones of monkey arm, horse leg, bat wing and seal flipper, have no direct relation to the species' present habits of life.
quote: by far the most important consideration is that the chief part of the organisation of every being is simply due to inheritance; and consequently, though each being assuredly is well fitted for its place in nature, many structures now have no direct relation to the habits of life of each species.
scope: all organisms
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic signal of morphological traits
proportion of morphological variance explained by phylogeny vs ecology
candidate_data: Phylogenetic comparative analyses of morphology vs ecology using AVONET or mammal trait databases (e.g. PanTHERIA) with TimeTree phylogenies.

label: No structure exists solely for the good of another species
claim: Natural selection cannot produce any structure in one species exclusively for the good of another species, though it can produce structures that harm other species; proof of such a structure would refute the theory.
quote: Natural selection cannot possibly produce any modification in any one species exclusively for the good of another species
scope: all interacting species
measurable_quantities: fitness effect on the bearer of traits that benefit other species
candidate_data: Mutualism and plant-pollinator interaction studies measuring costs and benefits to each partner; none known as a single dataset.

section: Organs not in all cases absolutely perfect.
label: Selection makes organisms only as perfect as their local competitors
claim: Natural selection only makes each organism as perfect as, or slightly more perfect than, the other inhabitants of its own country, so endemic species of a region such as New Zealand may yield to species introduced from a larger region.
quote: Natural selection tends only to make each organic being as perfect as, or slightly more perfect than, the other inhabitants of the same country with which it has to struggle for existence.
scope: inhabitants of regions, especially islands vs continents
measurable_quantities: success of introduced species by region of origin
decline of native species after introductions
candidate_data: GloNAF and Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species data on naturalisation success by donor region; Living Planet Index trends for island natives.

section: The law of Unity of Type and of the Conditions of Existence embraced by the theory of Natural Selection.
label: Unity of type is explained by unity of descent
claim: The fundamental agreement in structure among organisms of the same class, independent of their habits of life, is explained by their common descent.
quote: On my theory, unity of type is explained by unity of descent.
scope: organisms within the same class
measurable_quantities: congruence between morphological similarity and molecular phylogeny
candidate_data: Molecular phylogenies from GenBank and Open Tree of Life compared with morphological character matrices (MorphoBank).
